docs.title: Command line
docs.text: sadame has five commands: plan, apply and drift run a recipe, hosts shows which machines a selection reaches, and facts shows what recipes see on them. Each takes the same target and output options, so a command line that plans a change also applies it after replacing plan with apply. This page lists every command, option, environment variable and file; the exit codes have their own page.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
sadame plan examples/01-hello     # on this machine: what would change
sadame apply examples/01-hello    # make the change

sadame --help prints the same reference in short:

$ sadame --help
Usage: sadame COMMAND [RECIPE] [options]

Commands:
  plan     Show what apply would change, as a diff. Changes nothing.
  apply    Make the hosts match the recipe.
  drift    Like plan, but exit 1 when a host differs from the recipe.
  hosts    Show the selected hosts with their connection options and vars.
  facts    Show the facts recipes see on each host: CPUs, memory, addresses.

RECIPE is a recipe file or a directory containing recipe.rb
(default: ./recipe.rb). vars.rb and hosts.rb next to it are loaded if
present; hosts and facts only use those. Without -h, -g or --limit,
sadame runs on this machine.

Targets:
  -h, --host [USER@]HOST[:PORT],...   Run on these hosts over SSH
  -g, --group GROUP,...               Run on the hosts of these groups
  --limit GLOB                        Only hosts whose name matches, e.g. "web*"
  --inventory PATH                    Use this inventory instead of ./hosts.rb
  --sudo                              Run sadame with sudo on every target
  --forks N                           Work on at most N hosts at once (default: all)
  --serial N|N%                       Run in batches of N hosts (or N% of them), one
                                      batch after another; stop when a batch fails

Options:
  --var KEY=VALUE     Set vars[:KEY]; repeatable, overrides everything else
  --vars-file PATH    Load more vars from a Ruby file (local runs)
  --json              Print a JSON report instead of text
  --color             Always use colors
  --no-color          Never use colors (also: NO_COLOR environment variable)
  --host-name NAME    host_name in recipes and reports for local runs (default: local)
  --host-groups G,... host_groups in recipes for local runs
  --version           Print the version
  --help              Print this help

Exit status:
  0  success; for drift, every host matches the recipe
  1  apply failed, or drift found differences
  2  usage or recipe error, the state of a resource could not be read,
     or a host could not be reached

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
sadame COMMAND [RECIPE] [options]

Options may come before or after the command and the recipe.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Changes machines What it does plan no Reads the current state of every resource and prints what apply would change, as a diff. apply yes Changes what differs from the recipe, in order, then runs notifications. drift no Same comparison as plan; exits 1 when anything differs. For scripts and CI. hosts no Prints the selected hosts, their connection options and vars, and where each var came from. Connects to nothing. facts no Prints the facts recipes see: of this machine, or with -h, -g or --limit, of each selected host over SSH. Runs no recipe.

plan, apply and drift are explained together in plan, apply, drift.

docs.title: The recipe argument
docs.text:
Given sadame runs nothing ./recipe.rb a file, such as site.rb that file a directory, such as examples/01-hello recipe.rb in that directory

vars.rb and hosts.rb in the recipe's directory are loaded when they exist. Templates and files are looked up next to the recipe, then in its templates/ and files/ directories. hosts and facts do not need a recipe; given one, or a directory, they use the hosts.rb and vars.rb next to it.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
Without any of these options, sadame runs on the machine it is started on. With any of them, it runs on the selected hosts over SSH, copying itself and the recipe there first (see Remote hosts).

Option Value Effect -h, --host [USER@]HOST[:PORT], comma-separated These hosts. A name from the inventory keeps its settings; the user and port given here win. -g, --group group names, comma-separated The hosts of these groups in the inventory. --limit glob, such as "web*" Only the selected hosts whose name matches (* any characters, ? one). Alone, it filters every host of the inventory. --inventory path Use this inventory instead of hosts.rb next to the recipe. --sudo Run sadame with sudo on every target, whatever the inventory says. Needs passwordless sudo. Only with remote targets. --forks number Work on at most this many hosts at once (default: every selected host). Only with remote targets. --serial number, or percentage such as 25% Run the hosts in batches of this size, one batch after another, in the order they were selected. When a host of a batch fails or cannot be reached, the hosts of later batches are skipped. Only with remote targets.

-h and -g add up: -g db -h web1.example.com selects both. --limit narrows the result. Selection rules and vars precedence are in Inventory.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Effect --var KEY=VALUE Sets vars[:KEY]. Repeatable. Wins over every other source of vars. Whole numbers become Integers, true and false booleans; everything else stays a String. --vars-file PATH Loads more vars from a Ruby file that returns a Hash. Local runs only. --json Prints one JSON document instead of text; see JSON output. --color Always use colors, even when the output is not a terminal. --no-color Never use colors. --host-name NAME host_name in recipes and reports for local runs (default local). --host-groups G,... host_groups in recipes for local runs. --version Prints the version. --help Prints the help above. 
$ sadame --version
sadame 0.3.0

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Variable Effect NO_COLOR When set and not empty, no colors, as with --no-color. SADAME_BINARY_DIR Push mode: copy sadame-OS-ARCH from this directory to targets, instead of the running binary or a download. Used with binaries built from source. SADAME_DOWNLOAD_URL Push mode: download target binaries and SHA256SUMS from this URL instead of the GitHub release of the running version. TMPDIR Where sadame keeps the error output of the commands it runs while they run (default /tmp).

Every command sadame runs, on the machine itself or on a target, runs with LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, so its output is in English whatever the system's language (see exec).

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Path On What recipe.rb, vars.rb, hosts.rb your machine The recipe, its default vars, the inventory. templates/, files/ your machine Templates and files next to the recipe. ~/.sadame/dist/VERSION/ your machine Target binaries downloaded for push mode. ~/.sadame/bin/SHA256/sadame each target The copied binary, kept between runs and reused while its checksum matches.

Nothing else is left on a target; the copied recipe is removed after each run. Details in What is copied where.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
Preview a var change on one group. --var wins over hosts.rb, so a change can be tried without editing anything:

sadame plan site.rb -g db --var backup_hour=4

Roll out to part of a group first. Apply to the first web server, look at it, then apply to the rest:

sadame apply site.rb -g web --limit "web1*"
sadame apply site.rb -g web

Roll out one server at a time. With --serial 1, a change that breaks the first server stops before it reaches the second; --serial 25% keeps three quarters of the group untouched while the first quarter changes:

sadame apply site.rb -g web --serial 1

Check one machine that is not in the inventory. -h takes a full address, so a one-off check needs no hosts.rb:

sadame drift examples/07-hardening-baseline -h admin@203.0.113.10:2222 --sudo

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• -h for help. -h is --host and needs a value; use --help.

  • Misspelled options. sadame stops with exit status 2 instead of guessing:

    $ sadame plan examples/01-hello --colour
sadame: unknown option --colour
Run 'sadame --help' for usage.

$ echo $?
2

  • --sudo on a local run. It applies to remote targets only; run sudo sadame ... on the machine itself.

  • Expecting a list from --var. --var workers=8 gives the Integer 8, but --var ports=80,443 gives the String "80,443", which the recipe has to split.

docs.text:

  • JSON output

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Every sadame command ends with an exit status a script can act on: 0 when it did what was asked, 1 when apply failed or drift found a difference, and 2 when sadame could not do its job at all: a wrong command line, a broken recipe, a state it could not read, a host it could not reach. 2 never means "the machine differs"; a CI job can tell "the servers drifted" from "the check itself is broken".

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
sadame drift site.rb -g all
case $? in
  0) echo "every host matches" ;;
  1) echo "drift: run apply, or update the recipe" ;;
  *) echo "the check could not run" ; exit 2 ;;
esac

docs.title: By command
docs.text:
Status plan apply drift hosts 0 plan computed, with or without changes every resource and notification succeeded every host matches the recipe hosts listed 1 not used a resource or a notification failed a host differs from the recipe not used 2 usage or recipe error, a state could not be read, a host could not be reached usage or recipe error, a host could not be reached usage or recipe error, a state could not be read, a host could not be reached usage or inventory error

plan exits 0 even when there are changes: it answers "what would change", not "is anything different". Use drift for that question.

docs.title: Several hosts
docs.text:
With remote targets, each host gets a result, and the run exits with the highest status among them:

Host result Meaning Status ok sadame finished on the host with status 0 0 drift drift found a difference on the host 1 failed apply had a failed resource on the host 1 error sadame could not run on the host, or exited with 2 there 2 unreachable ssh could not connect 2

One host that drifted makes the whole run exit 1:

$ sadame drift site.rb --limit 'web*'
[web2.example.com] sadame 0.3.0 drift on web2.example.com (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))
[web1.example.com] sadame 0.3.0 drift on web1.example.com (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))
[web1.example.com]
[web2.example.com]
[web2.example.com] ~ file[/etc/demo-app/web.conf]
[web2.example.com]     --- /etc/demo-app/web.conf
[web2.example.com]     +++ /etc/demo-app/web.conf (desired)
[web2.example.com]     @@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
[web2.example.com]      # Managed by sadame.
[web2.example.com]      environment = production
[web2.example.com]     -workers     = 12
[web2.example.com]     +workers     = 8
[web2.example.com]
[web1.example.com] No drift: 6 resources match the recipe.
[web2.example.com] Drift: 1 of 6 resources differs from the recipe.

Hosts
  web1.example.com  ok
  web2.example.com  drift

drift on 2 hosts: 1 ok, 1 drift. Finished in 0.22s.

$ echo $?
1

One host that cannot be reached makes it exit 2, and the other hosts still run:

$ sadame plan site.rb -g db -h deploy@db2.example.com
[db1.example.com] sadame 0.3.0 plan on db1.example.com (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))
[db1.example.com]
[db1.example.com] Plan: 0 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 6 unchanged.

Hosts
  db1.example.com  ok
  db2.example.com  unreachable  connect failed: ssh: Could not resolve hostname db2.example.com: Name or service not known

plan on 2 hosts: 1 ok, 1 unreachable. Finished in 0.21s.

$ echo $?
2

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
Fail a scheduled CI job only on drift. Treat 1 and 2 differently, so a broken check does not look like drift (and drift does not look like a broken check). Drift in CI has complete GitHub Actions and GitLab CI pipelines.

Gate a deployment on a clean apply. In a shell script, set -e stops at the first failing host's exit status:

set -e
sadame apply site.rb -g db
sadame apply site.rb -g web

Read the status per host. --json reports each host's result and exit status, for when one number for the whole run is not enough (see JSON output).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Checking plan's status for changes. It is 0 either way; use drift.
  • Treating every non-zero status as drift. 2 means the check did not complete; the servers may be fine.
  • Unguarded exec resources. An exec without creates:, not_if: or only_if: always differs, so drift always exits 1.

docs.title: JSON output
docs.text: plan, apply and drift print a single JSON document with --json, instead of the human-readable report. It contains everything the text report shows: each resource's status and changes, the notifications, the summary counts, and the exit status. Nothing else is written to standard output, so it can be redirected to a file or piped into jq. Errors that stop sadame before a report exists (a bad option, a recipe that does not load) go to standard error, and standard output stays empty.

docs.title: Top level
docs.text: Field Type Description format_version integer Version of this format, currently 1. It changes when a field is removed or changes meaning; new fields may be added without a change. sadame_version string Version of sadame that wrote the report. command string "plan", "apply" or "drift". host string The machine the report is about; "local" for the machine sadame runs on. platform object See platform. resources array One resource object per declared resource, in recipe order. notifications array Notification runs during apply, in the order they ran. Always empty for plan and drift. summary object Number of resources per status; see statuses. Every status of the command is present, including those with 0. drift boolean or null plan and drift: true when at least one resource differs from the recipe. apply: null. failed boolean true when a resource failed, or for apply, a notification failed. exit_status integer The exit status of the command: see Plan, apply, drift. duration_seconds number Wall-clock time of the run, rounded to hundredths of a second.

docs.title: platform
docs.text: Field Type Description name string PRETTY_NAME from /etc/os-release, or "macOS". family string or null "debian", "rhel", "alpine", "arch", or null when unknown. package_manager string or null "apt", "dnf", "apk", "pacman", or null.

docs.title: resource
docs.text: Field Type Description id string type[name], as in the text output and in notifies:. type string "package", "file", "directory", "service", "exec" or "user". name string The resource name: package name, path, command, user name. status string See statuses. changes array Change objects. Empty when the resource is unchanged, failed before comparing, or skipped. notifications array plan and drift: what this resource would trigger. apply: what it triggered. Each has action, source, target and timing ("delayed" or "immediately"). error string or null Why the resource failed, or null.

docs.title: change
docs.text:
An attribute that differs. Most changes have from and to:

Field Type Description attribute string "state", "mode", "owner", "group", "enabled", "uid", "home", "shell", "groups" or "command". from string, integer, boolean, array or null Current value; null when the resource does not exist yet. to same Desired value. reason string Only on exec changes: why the command would run, for example "not_if exited non-zero".

File content changes carry a diff instead of the full text:

Field Type Description attribute string "content" sensitive boolean true when the file has sensitive: true. diff string or null Unified diff from current to desired, or null when sensitive.

docs.title: notification run
docs.text: Field Type Description action string The action, such as "reload" or "run". source string Id of the resource whose change triggered it. target string Id of the resource the action ran on. timing string "delayed" or "immediately". status string "ok" or "failed". error string or null Why it failed, or null.

docs.title: Statuses
docs.text: Command Status Meaning plan, drift create Does not exist yet. update Exists, some attributes differ. remove Exists, the recipe says state: :absent. run An exec whose guards say it must run. unchanged Matches the recipe. failed The current state could not be read; see error. apply changed Was changed. unchanged Already matched; nothing was done. failed Changing it failed; see error. skipped Not looked at, because an earlier resource or immediate notification failed.

docs.title: Push mode
docs.text:
When sadame runs on remote hosts (-h, -g, --limit), --json prints one document for the whole run. Each host's report, as described above, is nested under hosts:

Field Type Description format_version integer As above. sadame_version string Version of sadame on the machine that ran the push. command string "plan", "apply", "drift" or "facts". hosts array One object per host, in the order they were selected. hosts[].name string The host's name from the inventory or -h. hosts[].status string "ok", "drift", "failed", "error", "unreachable" or "skipped"; see Remote hosts. hosts[].exit_status integer or null That host's exit status; 2 when it could not be reached or prepared; null when it was skipped. hosts[].error string or null Why the host could not be reached or prepared, or sadame's error message. hosts[].report object or null The host's report; null when sadame did not run there. exit_status integer The highest exit status of all hosts: the run's exit status. duration_seconds number Wall-clock time of the whole run.

jq '.summary' drift.json

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reading failed as "drift found". failed means a resource could not be checked or changed. Drift is the drift field, and the exit status 1.
  • Parsing the text output. Its layout is for people and may change; the JSON fields are documented here and versioned by format_version.
  • Mixing standard error into the file. > drift.json 2>&1 or &> drift.json puts error messages into the JSON file. Redirect only standard output: > drift.json.

docs.title: directory
docs.text: directory makes sure a directory exists, with the permission bits and owner you give, or that it does not exist. Missing parent directories are created along the way. Use it before file resources that write into a new directory, and to keep application directories owned by the right user.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/directory/minimal.rb
directory "/srv/app"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description mode String of 3 or 4 octal digits unmanaged Permission bits, such as "0755". owner String unmanaged User name that owns the directory. group String unmanaged Group name of the directory. state :present or :absent :present :absent removes the directory. recursive true or false false With state: :absent, remove the directory and everything in it (rm -rf). Without it, only an empty directory can be removed (rmdir). notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

Creating runs mkdir -p, then chmod and chown for the attributes you gave. Parents created by mkdir -p get default permissions; declare them as their own resources if they matter.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
examples/resources/directory/recipe.rb
directory "/srv/app", mode: "0755"
directory "/srv/app/shared", owner: "www-data", group: "www-data", mode: "0750"

# Remove a directory and everything in it.
directory "/srv/app/tmp", state: :absent, recursive: true

unchanged  directory[/srv/app/tmp]

Summary

docs.title: Removing a directory
docs.text: The last resource in the recipe removes /srv/app/tmp and everything in it whenever it shows up. Without recursive: true, removing a directory that still has files in it fails with rmdir's error, which protects you from deleting more than you meant to.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Owner that does not exist yet. owner: "www-data" fails if the user is created later in the recipe, or by a package declared after the directory. Order the package or user resource first.
  • A file in the way. If the path exists as a regular file, the resource fails with "is a regular file, not a directory"; sadame does not delete it for you.
  • Expecting mode to apply to the contents. Only the directory itself is changed, never the files inside.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• file for files inside the directory.
  • user for the owner.

docs.title: exec
docs.text: exec runs a shell command. It is the escape hatch for anything the other resources do not cover: issuing a certificate, running an installer, installing from the AUR. A command has no state sadame can read, so to stay idempotent an exec needs a guard that says when the work is already done. Guards are evaluated during plan as well as apply; the command itself only runs during apply.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/exec/minimal.rb
exec "tar -czf /var/backups/etc.tar.gz /etc", creates: "/var/backups/etc.tar.gz"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description command String the resource name Command to run, when you want the name to be a short label. creates String none Skip when this path exists. not_if String none Skip when this command exits 0. only_if String none Skip unless this command exits 0. cwd String inherited Working directory for the command and its guards. env Hash of String to String none Environment variables for the command and its guards. action :run or :nothing :run :nothing never runs the command on its own, only when another resource notifies it. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this command runs. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

The command runs when every guard you gave agrees: the creates path is missing, not_if exits non-zero, and only_if exits 0. Guards are checked in that order and checking stops at the first one that says skip. Without any guard, the command runs on every apply.

Commands and guards run with /bin/sh and standard input closed. A command that exits non-zero fails the resource: apply prints the exit status and the command's error output, marks the resource failed, and skips the resources after it.

Every command sadame runs, including yours, runs in the C.UTF-8 locale (LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, LANGUAGE unset), so programs answer in English whatever the language of the machine or of the SSH session: a guard such as not_if: "ufw status | grep -q 'Status: active'" matches on every system. Set LC_ALL inside the command if it needs another locale.

Other resources can trigger the command with notifies: [:run, "exec[NAME]"]. Combined with action: :nothing, that gives a command that runs only when something else changed, such as systemctl daemon-reload after a unit file changed; see Notifications.

     creates: "/opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz"

# not_if: skip when the command succeeds.

     not_if: "grep -qs '^EDITOR=vim$' /etc/environment"

exec "git config --system init.defaultBranch main",
     only_if: "command -v git",

     cwd: "/opt/demo",

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No guard. An exec without creates, not_if or only_if runs on every apply, plan always lists it with "(no guard, runs on every apply)", and drift always reports it. Add a guard, or use action: :nothing if it should only run when notified.
  • Guards with side effects. Guards run during plan. A guard such as not_if: "mkdir /x" changes the machine when you only asked to look.
  • Interactive commands. Standard input is closed, so a command that prompts reads end-of-file and usually fails. Pass the tool's non-interactive flag (-y, --noconfirm).
  • A guard that never becomes true. If the command does not create what the guard checks for, it runs every time. Check the exact path or setting the command produces.

docs.title: file
docs.text: file manages a regular file: its content, permission bits and owner. The content comes from a string, an ERB template, or a file shipped next to the recipe. When the content differs, plan shows a unified diff of the file on disk against the desired content. On apply, new content is written to a temporary file in the same directory, given its final mode and owner, and renamed over the target, so programs reading the file never see it half written.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/file/minimal.rb
file "/etc/motd", content: "Authorized access only.\n"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description content String none The exact file content. template String none ERB template, rendered with vars, locals and facts. Looked up next to the recipe, then in its templates/ directory. Absolute paths are used as is. source String none File copied as is. Looked up next to the recipe, then in its files/ directory. locals Hash {} Values for the template, available as locals[:name]. Only with template:. mode String of 3 or 4 octal digits unmanaged Permission bits, such as "0644" or "0755". owner String unmanaged User name that owns the file. group String unmanaged Group name of the file. state :present or :absent :present :absent deletes the file. sensitive true or false false Hide content diffs in output and JSON, for files holding secrets. verify String containing %{path} none A command that checks the new content before it replaces the file, such as "visudo -cf %{path}". %{path} is the temporary file. If the command fails, the file is left as it was and the resource fails. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

Use at most one of content, template and source. With none of them, sadame manages only the attributes you give and creates an empty file if it is missing. Attributes you do not give are left alone; when the content is replaced, the file keeps its current mode, owner and group.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Numeric modes. mode: 644 is rejected. Ruby reads 644 as decimal, which is not the mode you mean; write mode: "0644".
  • Symlinks. If the path is a symbolic link, the resource fails with "is a symbolic link, not a regular file" instead of replacing the link. Manage the link's target path instead.
  • Missing parent directory. file does not create parent directories. Declare a directory resource before it.
  • Secrets in plan output. Without sensitive: true, the diff of a file holding credentials is printed and included in --json output.
  • Unchecked configuration files. A broken sudoers or sshd file can lock you out of a server. Give such files verify:; see examples/06-app-deploy-user.
  • Template next to the wrong recipe. Templates are found relative to the recipe file that declares the resource; see Recipe basics.

docs.title: git
docs.text:
git keeps a checkout of a git repository at a revision: a tag, a branch or a commit. The first apply clones the repository; later ones move the checkout when the revision points somewhere else, such as a branch that got new commits. Use it to deploy an application or a site from its repository, or to keep a tool's source on a machine.

New in 0.2.0

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/git/minimal.rb
package "git"
git "/opt/sadame", repository: "https://github.com/enderkus/sadame.git", revision: "v0.1.0"

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description repository String required The URL to clone, as git clone takes it: HTTPS, SSH (git@github.com:example/app.git) or a local path. revision String the remote's default branch A tag, a branch or a full 40-character commit. user String root Run every git command as this user (through su), so the checkout belongs to them and their SSH keys and git configuration apply. state :present or :absent :present :absent removes the checkout with rm -rf. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• plan asks the remote which commit the revision names (git ls-remote; tags first, then branches, as git resolves a name) and compares it with the checkout's HEAD. A full commit needs no remote. This is why plan and drift need network access to the repository.
  • apply clones with git clone --no-checkout, or fetches into an existing checkout, then runs git checkout --force --detach COMMIT. The checkout is on that commit, not on a branch.
  • A checkout whose origin URL differs from repository gets the new URL (git remote set-url) and is fetched from there.
  • An empty directory, such as one a directory resource created for the user, is cloned into. A directory with other files in it is an error.

git must be installed: declare package "git" before. On a machine where it is not installed yet, plan shows the revision as you wrote it; apply resolves it once the package is in.

Git never asks for a password or passphrase during a run (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0). Private repositories need credentials that work without a prompt, such as a deploy key in the user's ~/.ssh and the server's host key in their ~/.ssh/known_hosts.

docs.title: Following a branch, and restarting on a new commit
docs.text:
With a branch as the revision, every apply moves the checkout to the branch's latest commit, and a notification restarts the application only when it moved:

git "/srv/app",
    repository: "https://github.com/example/app.git",
    revision: "main",
    user: "deploy",
    notifies: [:restart, "service[app]"]

Pin a tag or a commit instead when every server must run the same code no matter when it was last applied.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Local changes in the checkout. Moving the checkout uses checkout --force, which discards changes to tracked files. Files git does not track, such as uploads or a .env, are kept. Keep anything that must survive outside the checkout.
  • Credentials that need a prompt. A private HTTPS repository without stored credentials, or an SSH host key that is not in known_hosts, fails instead of waiting for an answer that never comes.
  • The wrong user for the key. Without user:, git runs as root and uses root's ~/.ssh. With user: "deploy", the key must be deploy's.
  • Submodules. They are not cloned or updated. Run git submodule update --init from an exec resource that the git resource notifies.

docs.title: group
docs.text:
group makes sure a local group exists, with the gid you give, or that it does not exist. It reads the group with getent group and changes it with groupadd, groupmod and groupdel only when something differs. Members are set on the user side, with the user resource's groups:.

New in 0.2.0

docs.text:

group "app"

docs.text:
Option Type Default Description gid Integer unmanaged Numeric group ID. Changing it on an existing group runs groupmod -g; files keep their old gid. system true or false false Create a system group (groupadd -r), with a gid from the system range. Only used when the group is created. state :present or :absent :present :absent deletes the group with groupdel. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

On Alpine without the shadow package, sadame uses BusyBox's addgroup and delgroup instead. BusyBox cannot change a gid; declare package "shadow" first if you need to.

Declare the group before the users that join it; the user resource needs its groups to exist:

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A group that a user is still in. groupdel refuses to delete a group that is some user's primary group. Remove or change the user first.
  • A gid that is taken. groupadd -g and groupmod -g fail when another group already has that gid; the error names it.

docs.title: line
docs.text:
line manages one line in a file that something else owns, such as a setting in the configuration file a package installs, and leaves the rest of the file alone. When the file would change, plan shows the change as a diff of the file, and apply writes it in one rename, keeping the file's mode and owner.

Use file when sadame should own the whole file; use line when the package should keep owning it and you only need one setting.

New in 0.2.0

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description path String required Absolute path of the file to edit. line String the name The line, without a newline. Give it when the name is a description, or when the same line goes into two files. match Regexp, or a String with one none Lines to replace. Every line that matches is replaced by the line; when none matches and the line is not in the file, it is appended. state :present or :absent :present :absent removes the line, and every line that matches match. verify String containing %{path} none A command that checks the new content before it replaces the file, such as "sshd -t -f %{path}". If it fails, the file is not changed. sensitive true or false false Hide the diff in output and JSON, for lines with secrets. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

Without match, the line is appended when no line in the file is exactly the same. Lines are compared without their newline; spaces count.

The file must exist when the change is applied: line edits files, it does not create them. On a machine where the file comes from a package that the same recipe installs, plan shows the line being added to a file that "does not exist yet", and apply edits the file the package created.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
examples/resources/line/recipe.rb
# The SSH server's configuration belongs to its package. Each line resource
# changes one line and leaves the rest of the file as it was shipped, and
# sshd -t checks the edited file before it replaces the real one.
package({ "arch" => "openssh" }.fetch(platform.family, "openssh-server"))
# sshd -t needs host keys and, on Debian and Ubuntu, /run/sshd. Most
# packages leave both to the service's first start.
exec "ssh-keygen -A", creates: "/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key"
directory "/run/sshd", mode: "0755" if platform.family == "debian"

# Replaces the line that sets the option, commented out or not; appends it
# when no line does.
line "PermitRootLogin no",
     path: "/etc/ssh/sshd_config",
     match: /^#?\s*PermitRootLogin\s/,
     verify: "sshd -t -f %{path}"

line "PasswordAuthentication no",
     path: "/etc/ssh/sshd_config",
     match: /^#?\s*PasswordAuthentication\s/,
     verify: "sshd -t -f %{path}"

# Removes the line if it is there. Debian ships it; sshd's default is "no".
line "no X11 forwarding",
     path: "/etc/ssh/sshd_config",
     line: "X11Forwarding yes",
     state: :absent,
     verify: "sshd -t -f %{path}"

docs.title: Writing match
docs.text:
match is a regular expression for one line, without its newline. Make it match every form the setting can take in the file, commented out or not, with or without spaces, so that the line replaces the setting instead of being appended after it:

You want match Port 2222 where the file has #Port 22 /^#?\s*Port\s/ vm.swappiness = 10 where the file may have vm.swappiness=60 /^#?\s*vm\.swappiness\s*=/ include_dir = 'conf.d' in postgresql.conf /^#?\s*include_dir\s*=/

When more than one line matches, every one of them is replaced, so the file ends up with the same line twice rather than two different values.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Managing the same file with file and line. The file resource writes the whole content on every run and line changes it again, so neither ever reports "unchanged". Use one or the other.
  • A match that misses the active setting. If the file has PermitRootLogin yes and match is /^#PermitRootLogin/, nothing matches, so PermitRootLogin no is appended at the end, and sshd keeps the first value it reads: yes. Cover both forms: /^#?\s*PermitRootLogin\s/.
  • Expecting line to create the file. It fails with "does not exist". Create the file with file, or install the package that ships it, earlier in the recipe.

docs.text:

docs.title: link
docs.text:
link makes sure a symbolic link exists and points where you say, or that it does not exist. It reads the link with readlink, creates or repoints it with ln -sfn, and removes it with rm -f. Use it for the classic "enabled" links (sites-enabled/app), for a current link between releases, and to put a program on the PATH.

New in 0.2.0

docs.text: link "/etc/nginx/sites-enabled/app", to: "/etc/nginx/sites-available/app"

docs.text:
Option Type Default Description to String required Where the link points. Stored as given: a relative target such as "releases/2" is relative to the link's directory. The target does not have to exist. state :present or :absent :present :absent removes the link. force true or false false Replace a regular file that is where the link should be. Without it, a file in the way is an error. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

The link's directory must exist; declare it with a directory resource first if it does not. A directory where the link should be is always an error, even with force: true.

docs.title: Reloading a service when a link changes
docs.text:
A link that enables a configuration can notify the service that reads it:

     notifies: [:reload, "service[nginx]"]

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A file in the way. A path that exists as a regular file fails with "is a regular file, not a symbolic link". Add force: true when replacing it is what you want, as for /etc/resolv.conf.

docs.title: package
docs.text: package makes sure a system package is installed, or not installed. Sadame reads /etc/os-release to pick the package manager, so the same recipe works on Debian and Ubuntu (apt), Rocky, AlmaLinux and Fedora (dnf), Alpine (apk), and Arch and Arch-based systems such as Omarchy (pacman). Before acting it asks the package manager whether the package is installed, and only installs or removes when the answer differs from the recipe.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/package/minimal.rb
package "htop"

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description state :installed or :absent :installed Whether the package must be installed. options String or Array of Strings none Extra flags for the install or remove command, placed before the package name. A String is used as is; Array elements are each shell-quoted. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

docs.title: Commands per package manager
docs.text:
NAME is the package name, OPTIONS the options: value.

Manager Detected on Installed when Install Remove apt ID or ID_LIKE is debian, ubuntu dpkg-query -W -f='${Status}' NAME ends in installed DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y OPTIONS NAME DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get remove -y OPTIONS NAME dnf rhel, centos, fedora, rocky, almalinux, ol rpm -q NAME exits 0 dnf install -y OPTIONS NAME dnf remove -y OPTIONS NAME apk alpine apk info -e NAME exits 0 apk add OPTIONS NAME apk del OPTIONS NAME pacman arch, archarm, manjaro, endeavouros pacman -Q NAME exits 0 pacman -S --needed --noconfirm OPTIONS NAME pacman -Rns --noconfirm OPTIONS NAME

Index refreshes:

  • apt: DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get update runs once per apply, right before the first install. Runs that install nothing never touch the network.
  • dnf and apk refresh their metadata themselves.
  • pacman: sadame never runs pacman -Sy. Refreshing the sync database without upgrading (-Sy without -u) is a partial upgrade, which Arch does not support. Keep the system upgraded with pacman -Syu as usual.

docs.title: AUR packages
docs.text:
The package resource does not install from the AUR in this release. Until it does, use an AUR helper such as yay or paru through exec, guarded so it only runs when the package is missing:

examples/resources/package/aur.rb
# AUR packages are not handled by the package resource in sadame 0.1. Use an
# AUR helper through exec, guarded so it only runs when the package is
# missing and the helper is installed. yay and paru refuse to run as root,
# so the command runs as the user named in vars[:aur_user].
exec "runuser -u #{vars[:aur_user]} -- yay -S --needed --noconfirm visual-studio-code-bin",
     only_if: "command -v yay",
     not_if: "pacman -Q visual-studio-code-bin"
examples/resources/package/vars.rb
# The AUR helper must run as a normal user. When sadame runs through sudo,
# SUDO_USER is the user who called it.
{
  aur_user: ENV["SUDO_USER"] || ENV["USER"]
}

AUR helpers refuse to run as root, which is why the command goes through runuser. The helper then calls sudo pacman itself, so that user needs to be able to run pacman with sudo without a password prompt: sadame runs commands with standard input closed and cannot answer one. Without yay installed, only_if skips the resource:

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/package/aur.rb

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Fresh Arch containers have no sync database. In the archlinux Docker image, pacman -S warns "database file for 'core' does not exist" and fails with "target not found" until pacman -Syu has run once. Installed systems do not have this problem.
  • Package groups and virtual packages. The installed check asks for the exact name. A group such as base-devel on Arch, or a name that is only provided by another package, never reports as installed, so it shows up in every plan. Declare the member packages instead.
  • Expecting upgrades. state: :installed means "some version is installed". Sadame does not upgrade packages in this release.
  • Mixing families without a condition. package "apache2" on Rocky fails at apply time with the package manager's own error.

docs.title: service
docs.text: service manages a service: whether it starts at boot (enable) and whether it is running now (state). It works with systemd, and with OpenRC on Alpine. It reads the current state with systemctl is-enabled and systemctl is-active (or rc-update show and rc-service NAME status) and only changes what differs. Other resources can ask a service to reload or restart when they change, through notifies:.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/service/recipe.rb
# On Arch, installing nginx does not enable or start it; the service
# resource does. Debian and Ubuntu start services on install, so there the
# same resource usually reports no change.
package "nginx"
service "nginx", enable: true, state: :running

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description enable true or false unmanaged Start at boot (systemctl enable) or not (systemctl disable). Enabled means systemctl is-enabled prints enabled. state :running or :stopped unmanaged Running now (systemctl start) or not (systemctl stop). Running means systemctl is-active prints active. user String none Manage the unit in this user's systemd instance (systemctl --user -M USER@), such as a unit in ~/.config/systemd/user/. The user must be logged in or have lingering enabled (loginctl enable-linger USER). systemd only. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

A service with neither option manages nothing by itself; it is still a valid target for notifications.

docs.text:

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No service manager. The resource needs systemd or OpenRC running. In most containers neither runs, and it fails with "no service manager is running on this host".
  • Declaring the service before its package. On a fresh machine the unit does not exist yet, so plan shows it as disabled and stopped, and apply fails if the package comes later in the recipe. Put package first.
  • Units that cannot be enabled. systemctl is-enabled prints static for units without an [Install] section. Those never count as enabled, so enable: true on them shows a change on every plan. Leave enable out.
  • Expecting a reload when only the service changed. reload and restart happen only through notifications from other resources.
  • Reloading a service that cannot reload. systemctl reload fails for units without ExecReload=, and rc-service NAME reload for init scripts without a reload command. Notify :restart for those.
  • Different names on different systems. The SSH server is ssh on Debian and Ubuntu and sshd elsewhere; cron is cron, crond or cronie. Pick the name from platform.family.

docs.title: user
docs.text: user manages a local Linux user account: whether it exists, its UID, home directory, login shell, and the groups it must belong to. It reads the account with getent passwd and id -nG, and changes it with useradd, usermod and userdel only when something differs.

Option Type Default Description uid Integer unmanaged Numeric user ID. home String unmanaged Home directory path. shell String unmanaged Login shell, such as "/bin/bash" or "/usr/sbin/nologin". groups Array of Strings unmanaged Groups the user must belong to. Other memberships are left alone. The groups must exist. system true or false false Create a system account (useradd -r), which gets no home directory. Only used when the user is created. state :present or :absent :present :absent deletes the account with userdel; the home directory is kept. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

New users that are not system users get a home directory (useradd -m). Changing home on an existing user updates the account but does not move files.
